content.heading: 8.4 Hyperplanes
content.paragraph: Hyperplanes play a special role in the geometry of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ because they divide the space into two disjoint pieces, just as a plane separates $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ into two parts and a line cuts through $\text{ℝ}^{2}$. The key to working with hyperplanes is to use simple implicit descriptions, rather than the explicit or parametric representations of lines and planes used in the earlier work with affine sets.1

An implicit equation of a line in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ has the form $ax + by = d$. An implicit equation of a plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ has the form $ax + by + cz = d$. Both equations describe the line or plane as the set of all points at which a linear expression (also called a linear functional) has a fixed value, $d$.﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A linear functional on $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a linear transformation $f$ from $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ into $\text{ℝ}$. For each scalar $d$ in $\text{ℝ}$, the symbol $\text{[}\textit{f\,\,}\text{:\,\,\,}d\text{]}$ denotes the set of all $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ at which the value of $f$ is $d$. That is,
The zero functional is the transformation such that $f(\textbf{x}) = 0$ for all $\textbf{x}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. All other linear functionals on $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ are said to be nonzero.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: In $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, the line $x - 4y = 13$ is a hyperplane in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$, and it is the set of points at which the linear functional $f(x,y) = x - 4y$ has the value $13$. That is, the line is the set $\lbrack f:13\rbrack$.﻿

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: In $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, the plane $5x - 2y + 3z = 21$ is a hyperplane, the set of points at which the linear functional $g(x,y,z) = 5x - 2y + 3z$ has the value $21$. This hyperplane is the set $\lbrack g:21\rbrack$.﻿

Then $\lbrack f:0\rbrack = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \text{ℝ}^{n}:\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} = 0 \right\}$, which shows that $\lbrack f:0\rbrack$ is the orthogonal complement of the subspace spanned by $\textbf{n}\text{.}$ In the terminology of calculus and geometry for $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, $\textbf{n}$ is called a normal vector to $\lbrack f:0\rbrack$. (A “normal” vector in this sense need not have unit length.) Also, $\textbf{n}$ is said to be normal to each parallel hyperplane $\lbrack f:d\rbrack$, even though $\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x}$ is not zero when $d \neq 0$.﻿
Another name for $\lbrack f:d\rbrack$ is a level set of $f$, and $\textbf{n}$ is sometimes called the gradient of $f$ when $f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x}$ for each $\textbf{x}$.﻿

example.paragraph: $H_{1}$ is parallel to a plane $H_{0}$ through the origin that contains the translated points

Since these two points are linearly independent, $H_{0} = \text{Span}\left\{ \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$. Let $\textbf{n} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$ be the normal to $H_{0}$. Then $\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1}$ are each orthogonal to $\textbf{n}$. That is, $(\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$ and $\left( \textbf{v}_{3} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right) \cdot \textbf{n} = 0$. These two equations form a system whose augmented matrix can be row reduced:

Row operations yield $a = \left( - \frac{2}{4} \right)c$, $b = \left( \frac{5}{4} \right)c$, with $c$ free. Set $c = 4$, for instance. Then $\textbf{n} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} {- 2} \\ 5 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$ and $H_{0} = \text{[}\textit{f\,\,}\text{:\,\,\,0]}$, where $f\left( \textbf{x} \right) = - 2x_{1} + 5x_{2} + 4x_{3}$.﻿

The parallel hyperplane $H_{1}$ is $\lbrack f:d\rbrack$. To find $d$, use the fact that $\textbf{v}_{1}$ is in $H_{1}$, and compute $d = f\left( \textbf{v}_{1} \right) = f(1,1,1) = - 2(1) + 5(1) + 4(1) = 7$. As a check, compute $f\left( \textbf{v}_{2} \right) = f(2, - 1,4) = - 2(2) + 5( - 1) + 4(4) = 16 - 9 = 7$. Observe $f(\textbf{v}_{3}) = 7$ also.

So far, every hyperplane examined has been described as $\lbrack f:d\rbrack$ for some linear functional $f$ and some $d$ in $\text{ℝ}$, or equivalently as $\left\{ \textbf{x} \in \text{ℝ}^{n}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = d \right\}$ for some $\textbf{n}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. The following theorem shows that every hyperplane has these equivalent descriptions.

note.title: Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.paragraph: A subset $H$ of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a hyperplane if and only if $H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$ for some nonzero linear functional $f$ and some scalar $d$ in $\text{ℝ}$. Thus, if $H$ is a hyperplane, there exist a nonzero vector $\textbf{n}$ and a real number $d$ such that $H = \left\{ \textbf{x}:\textbf{n} \cdot \textbf{x} = d \right\}$.﻿

Many important applications of hyperplanes depend on the possibility of “separating” two sets by a hyperplane. Intuitively, this means that one of the sets is on one side of the hyperplane and the other set is on the other side. The following terminology and notation will help to make this idea more precise.

note.title: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts
note.heading: Topology in ℝn﻿: Terms and Facts
note.paragraph: For any point $\textbf{p}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ and any real $\delta > 0$, the open ball $B(\textbf{p},\delta)$ with center $\textbf{p}$ and radius $\delta$ is given by

Given a set $S$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, a point $\textbf{p}$ is an interior point of $S$ if there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $B\left( \textbf{p},\delta \right) \subseteq S$. If every open ball centered at $\textbf{p}$ intersects both $S$ and the complement of $S$, then $\textbf{p}$ is called a boundary point of $S$. A set is open if it contains none of its boundary points. (This is equivalent to saying that all of its points are interior points.) A set is closed if it contains all of its boundary points. (If $S$ contains some but not all of its boundary points, then $S$ is neither open nor closed.) A set $S$ is bounded if there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $S \subseteq B\left( \textbf{0},\delta \right)$. A set in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is compact if it is closed and bounded.
Theorem:The convex hull of an open set is open, and the convex hull of a compact set is compact. (The convex hull of a closed set need not be closed. See Exercise 33.)

content.paragraph: Notice that strict separation requires that the two sets be disjoint, while mere separation does not. Indeed, if two circles in the plane are externally tangent, then their common tangent line separates them (but does not separate them strictly).
Although it is necessary that two sets be disjoint in order to strictly separate them, this condition is not sufficient, even for closed convex sets. For example, let

Then $A$ and $B$ are disjoint closed convex sets, but they cannot be strictly separated by a hyperplane (line in $\text{ℝ}^{2}$). See Figure 4. Thus the problem of separating (or strictly separating) two sets by a hyperplane is more complex than it might at first appear.

content.paragraph: There are many interesting conditions on the sets $A$ and $B$ that imply the existence of a separating hyperplane, but the following two theorems are sufficient for this section. The proof of the first theorem requires quite a bit of preliminary material,3 but the second theorem follows easily from the first.

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem ﻿12﻿
note.paragraph: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are nonempty convex sets such that $A$ is compact and $B$ is closed. Then there exists a hyperplane $H$ that strictly separates $A$ and $B$ if and only if $A \cap B = \varnothing$.﻿

note.title: ﻿﻿Theorem 13﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿Theorem 13﻿
note.paragraph: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are nonempty compact sets. Then there exists a hyperplane that strictly separates $A$ and $B$ if and only if $\text{(conv~}A\text{)} \cap \text{(conv~}B\text{)} = \varnothing$.﻿

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Suppose that $\text{(conv~}A\text{)} \cap \text{(conv~}B\text{)} = \varnothing$. Since the convex hull of a compact set is compact, Theorem 12 ensures that there is a hyperplane $H$ that strictly separates $\text{conv}A$ and $\text{conv~}B$. Clearly, $H$ also strictly separates the smaller sets $A$ and $B$.﻿

Conversely, suppose the hyperplane $H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$ strictly separates $A$ and $B$. Without loss of generality, assume that $f(A) < d$ and $f(B) > d$. Let $\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{x}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{x}_{k}$ be any convex combination of elements of $A$. Then

since $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$. Thus $f\left( \text{conv~}A \right) < d$. Likewise, $f\left( \text{conv~}B \right) > d$, so $H = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$ strictly separates $\text{conv}A$ and $\text{conv~}B$. By Theorem 12, $\text{conv~}A$ and $\text{conv~}B$ must be disjoint.

example.paragraph: Let

Show that the hyperplane $H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$, where $f\left( x_{1},x_{2},x_{3} \right) = 2x_{1} - 3x_{2} + x_{3}$, does not separate $A$ and $B$. Is there a hyperplane parallel to $H$ that does separate $A$ and $B$? Do the convex hulls of $A$ and $B$ intersect?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Evaluate the linear functional $f$ at each of the points in $A$ and $B$:
Since $f(\textbf{b}_{1}) = 4$ is less than $5$ and $f(\textbf{b}_{2}) = 12$ is greater than $5$, points of $B$ lie on both sides of $H = \lbrack f:5\rbrack$ and so $H$ does not separate $A$ and $B$.﻿
Since $f(A) < 3$ and $f(B) > 3$, the parallel hyperplane $\lbrack f:3\rbrack$ strictly separates $A$ and $B$. By Theorem 13, $\text{(conv~}A\text{)} \cap \text{(conv~}B\text{)} = \varnothing$.﻿

Caution: If there were no hyperplane parallel to $H$ that strictly separated $A$ and $B$, this would not necessarily imply that their convex hulls intersect. It might be that some other hyperplane not parallel to $H$ would strictly separate them.
